questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Define a recessive allele
questions.stem: A survey of a moth population starts by recording how the pale and dark wing forms are inherited.

options.text: A recessive allele is one whose effect is masked when a dominant allele is present in the same individual.
A recessive allele is one that appears only when the organism lives in a cold and dry season.
options.misconception: believes recessiveness depends on the environment

options.text: A recessive allele is one that is copied less often than the dominant allele during gamete formation.
options.misconception: confuses allele recessiveness with copy number

options.text: A recessive allele is one that must be inherited from both parents before it can be passed on.
options.misconception: believes a recessive allele cannot be transmitted by a carrier

questions.explanation: Recessive describes how an allele shows up alongside a dominant one in a heterozygote, not how often it is copied. A recessive allele can still be carried and passed on by an unaffected parent.
questions.hint: Focus on what happens in a heterozygote.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a sample is tested against a predicted ratio
questions.stem: Field teams must learn how to test whether an observed split of offspring matches a predicted ratio.

options.text: By checking whether each class count equals the ratio exactly, since ratios are exact counts.
options.misconception: treats a predicted ratio as a set of exact counts

options.text: By comparing observed counts with the proportions a ratio predicts and asking whether deviations are plausible.
By repeating the count until the observed numbers match the predicted numbers exactly.
options.misconception: believes the sample must be repeated until it matches

options.text: By counting only the class with the most individuals and ignoring the rest of the sample.
options.misconception: ignores every class except the largest one

questions.explanation: A ratio gives expected proportions, so a test compares the sample with those proportions and asks whether the difference is within random variation. Repeating until the counts match exactly tests nothing.
questions.hint: Think about sampling variation, not exact equality.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Check a dihybrid harvest against the 9:3:3:1 ratio
questions.stem: The survey log for one pond records offspring of a dihybrid cross: 108 showed both dominant traits, 36 one, 36 the other and 12 neither.

options.text: The counts fit the 1:2:1 ratio, so only one gene is segregating in this population.
options.misconception: reads a dihybrid harvest as a single gene cross

options.text: The counts fit the 3:1 ratio, so the second trait is inherited but not scored.
options.misconception: assumes a second trait was simply not scored

options.text: The counts fit a 1:1 split, so the two genes are inherited as a single unit.
options.misconception: claims complete linkage from a nine to three ratio

options.text: The counts fit the 9:3:3:1 ratio, so the two genes assort independently.

questions.explanation: Scaling the 9:3:3:1 ratio to 192 offspring gives 108:36:36:12, exactly the logged counts. That match is the evidence for independent assortment of the two genes in the sampled population.
questions.hint: Scale the four-term ratio to the sample size.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Correct a misreading of a Punnett square
questions.stem: One method sheet is rejected because it reads a two by two Punnett square for Aa by Aa as giving four different offspring.

options.text: The sheet is fine, because a Punnett square lists every possible offspring type separately.
options.misconception: believes each cell of the square is a separate class

options.text: The sheet should say the square gives four equally likely outcomes for the four offspring.
options.misconception: claims four equal classes from a monohybrid square

options.text: The sheet is wrong, because the square gives four cells but only three distinct genotypes.
The sheet should say the square covers two different crosses rather than one.
options.misconception: misreads the grid as combining two separate crosses

questions.explanation: A monohybrid Punnett square has four cells, but two carry the same allele combination, so only three genotype classes appear. Reading the grid as four classes is a counting error.
questions.hint: Two of the four cells hold the same combination.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the expected recessive class size
questions.stem: The survey needs a figure for the number of recessive offspring expected in 300 progeny from two heterozygous parents.
questions.explanation: Two heterozygous parents give a 3:1 phenotypic ratio, so one quarter of the 300 progeny are expected to show the recessive trait. One quarter of 300 is 75, and a count near 75 is unremarkable.
questions.hint: One quarter of the progeny in this cross.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Count recessive seedlings predicted by dominance
questions.stem: Another tally in the survey notes records 480 seedlings from a cross of two heterozygous plants and asks how many should show the recessive trait.
questions.explanation: Only the homozygous recessive class is unmasked, so one quarter of the 480 seedlings shows the recessive trait. One quarter of 480 is 120, so a count near that is expected.
questions.hint: Only homozygous recessive seedlings look recessive.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how unaffected parents produce recessive offspring
questions.stem: The write-up should explain in words why a survey can find unaffected parents producing recessive offspring.

answer.exemplar: Two unaffected parents can each be heterozygous, carrying a recessive allele that is masked by the dominant allele they also carry. When such parents mate, a quarter of the offspring receive two recessive alleles and show the recessive trait, so the trait reappears even though neither parent showed it.

questions.explanation: Recessive traits reappear because heterozygotes carry the recessive allele without showing it. Two carriers produce one quarter homozygous recessive offspring, so unaffected parents can give affected young.
questions.hint: Think about parents who carry the allele unseen.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a 3:1 pattern needs heterozygous parents
questions.stem: A survey protocol asks why the 3:1 pattern is expected only when both parents are heterozygous.

options.text: Because a 3:1 pattern appears only when the dominant allele is completely lethal when homozygous.
options.misconception: invents a lethal dominant allele to explain the ratio

options.text: Because a 3:1 pattern appears only in the first generation of any cross between unlike plants.
options.misconception: mislocates the ratio in the first generation

options.text: Because the recessive quarter appears only when each parent can contribute the recessive allele.
Because a 3:1 pattern appears only when the environment favours the recessive phenotype.
options.misconception: blames environmental selection for the expected ratio

questions.explanation: The recessive class in a 3:1 ratio is the homozygous recessive quarter, and it appears only if both parents carry the recessive allele. Heterozygous parents do that while still showing the dominant phenotype.
questions.hint: The recessive quarter must be reachable from both parents.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose of a recessive tester
questions.stem: Notes from the sampling trip explain why the field team uses a recessive tester in a testcross.

options.text: Because a recessive tester cannot produce any dominant offspring, so the sample stays easier to score.
options.misconception: describes the tester's colour, not its genetic role

options.text: Because the recessive tester passes on only recessive alleles, so the unknown parent's alleles stay visible.
Because a recessive tester produces more offspring than a dominant tester under field conditions.
options.misconception: claims the tester changes the number of offspring

options.text: Because a recessive tester guarantees that only one gene is segregating in the cross.
options.misconception: restricts testcrosses to single gene inheritance

questions.explanation: A homozygous recessive tester contributes only recessive alleles, so it cannot mask the alleles the unknown parent supplies. The offspring phenotypes therefore report the unknown parent's gametes directly.
questions.hint: Ask what the tester always passes on.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret three colour classes in a plant population
questions.stem: Researchers counted 320 flowering plants and scored 200 as red, 80 as white and 40 as pale pink.

options.text: The pale class fits carriers of two partially dominant alleles, while red and white fit the homozygous classes.
The counts show three different alleles at the locus, one for each flower colour.
options.misconception: confuses three phenotype classes with three alleles

options.text: The counts show that the red flowers are all heterozygous, since half of the sample is red.
options.misconception: treats a large class as evidence of heterozygosity

options.text: The counts show the population is not breeding true, because the three colours appear together.
options.misconception: reads three colour classes as proof of unstable breeding

questions.explanation: With two partially dominant alleles, the homozygotes give the two pure colours and the heterozygotes the intermediate one, so 320 plants should show a rough 1:2:1 split. Three colours do not mean three alleles.
questions.hint: Intermediate colour usually signals a heterozygote.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Correct a claim that recessive traits skip generations
questions.stem: A paragraph of the field notes returns marked because it claims a recessive trait can never appear in the offspring of two dominant-looking plants.

options.text: The paragraph is correct, because dominant-looking plants cannot carry a recessive allele at all.
options.misconception: believes dominant appearance rules out recessive alleles

options.text: The paragraph should say the trait appears only if both dominant-looking plants are pure breeding.
options.misconception: requires both parents to be homozygous to explain the trait

options.text: The paragraph should say the trait can appear only after two further generations of inbreeding.
options.misconception: invents extra generations before recessive traits appear

options.text: The paragraph is wrong, because two heterozygous dominant-looking plants can produce recessive offspring.

questions.explanation: A dominant-looking plant may be heterozygous and still carry the recessive allele, so two such plants can produce homozygous recessive offspring in about one quarter of the brood. Pure breeding is not required.
questions.hint: Dominant-looking plants can still carry the allele.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the expected recessive quarter for a sample
questions.stem: The protocol asks the team to calculate how many of 400 offspring should show the recessive trait in a cross of two heterozygotes.
questions.explanation: A 3:1 phenotypic ratio puts one quarter of the offspring in the recessive class. One quarter of 400 is 100 offspring, which is the figure the survey should compare its field counts against.
questions.hint: Compare with the recessive quarter of the ratio.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Count a single dominant class in a dihybrid cross
questions.stem: The tally sheet asks how many of 240 offspring of two double heterozygotes should show only one dominant trait.
questions.explanation: In a dihybrid cross each single-dominant class holds three sixteenths of the offspring, so 240 times three sixteenths is 90. The double dominant class would be nine sixteenths, or 135 offspring.
questions.hint: Each single dominant class is three sixteenths.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Describe how a Punnett square is read
questions.stem: For the discussion of recessive alleles the report asks the team to describe how a Punnett square is read.

answer.exemplar: A Punnett square lists the gamete types along the top and down the side, and each cell holds the allele pair that results from one combination. Reading across all cells and grouping cells with the same pair gives the expected genotype classes and their proportions, such as three dominant to one recessive for a cross of two heterozygotes.

questions.explanation: The columns and rows stand for the gametes each parent can make, and every cell is one possible allele pair. Counting identical cells gives genotype classes, and dominance converts them into visible traits.
questions.hint: Each cell is one gamete pairing.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the commonest error when reading a field ratio
questions.stem: A protocol asks the team to describe the most common error when reading a field ratio.

options.text: Reading an expected ratio as a fixed set of counts instead of proportions to compare with a sample.
Counting the largest class first, since the largest class carries the most reliable information.
options.misconception: prioritises the largest class and ignores the others

options.text: Discarding the smallest class, since rare phenotypes are usually misidentified in the field.
options.misconception: drops the rarest class as if it were misidentified

options.text: Converting the counts into percentages early, since percentages hide the sample size.
options.misconception: believes percentages remove the need for sample size

questions.explanation: Ratios describe proportions, so a sample rarely matches them exactly and small deviations are normal. Discarding classes or ignoring the sample size turns the comparison into a guess rather than a test.
questions.hint: Ask whether the counts are being compared with proportions.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Compare what dominant and recessive phenotypes reveal about parents
questions.stem: Field biologists want to know why a recessive-looking individual proves less about its parents than a dominant one.

options.text: Because recessive-looking individuals are rarer, so their parents are harder to find.
options.misconception: links phenotype visibility to how common the class is

options.text: Because a recessive phenotype needs a recessive allele from both parents, while a dominant one needs only one.
Because dominant-looking individuals are usually the offspring of inbred stock.
options.misconception: blames recessive appearance on the parents being inbred

options.text: Because recessive phenotypes develop later, so the parents cannot be scored.
options.misconception: claims recessive phenotypes develop too late to score

questions.explanation: A recessive phenotype means both parents supplied a recessive allele, so it narrows the possible parental genotypes to carriers. A dominant phenotype only proves one parent supplied a dominant allele.
questions.hint: Count the parents that must carry the allele.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Identify a carrier from testcross offspring counts
questions.stem: A note records a testcross in which 38 offspring showed the dominant form and 42 showed the recessive form.

options.text: The counts fit a 3:1 ratio, so the unknown parent must have been homozygous dominant.
options.misconception: reads a near even split as a three to one ratio

options.text: The counts fit a 9:3:3:1 ratio, so two genes are segregating in this cross.
options.misconception: claims a dihybrid ratio from a single trait cross

options.text: The counts fit a 1:2:1 ratio, so the unknown parent produced three gamete types.
options.misconception: mistakes a genotypic ratio for the gamete output

options.text: The counts fit a 1:1 ratio, so the unknown parent was a heterozygous carrier.

questions.explanation: The recessive tester contributes only recessive alleles, so the near 38:42 split shows the unknown parent produced dominant and recessive gametes in equal numbers. Only a heterozygote does that, so it is a carrier.
questions.hint: Split the offspring by the two visible forms.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Correct a claim that ratios are exact in field samples
questions.stem: The survey methods are challenged because they describe the recessive class of a field population as exactly one quarter of every sample.

options.text: The methods are fine, because the ratio is set by genetics and not by sampling at all.
options.misconception: treats genetics as removing sampling variation

options.text: The methods should say the recessive class is exactly one quarter only in the second generation.
options.misconception: pins the exact ratio to one particular generation

options.text: The methods are wrong, because one quarter is an expected proportion and field samples vary around it.
The methods should say the recessive class grows steadily until it reaches one quarter.
options.misconception: believes the recessive class climbs to a fixed share

questions.explanation: Ratios are expectations over many offspring, so any field sample of a few dozen individuals can fall well above or below the one quarter mark. Reporting the sample figure with its deviation is the honest approach.
questions.hint: Expectations and sample values are not the same.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the recessive half of a testcross sample
questions.stem: The protocol asks the team to calculate how many of 90 testcross offspring from a carrier would show the recessive form.
questions.explanation: A testcross of a carrier with a homozygous recessive gives a 1:1 phenotypic ratio, so half of the 90 offspring show the recessive form. Half of 90 is 45, the figure to compare with the field counts.
questions.hint: Half the offspring match the tester form.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the chance of a recessive offspring from two carriers
questions.stem: One entry in the log asks for the probability that a random offspring of two carriers shows the recessive trait.
questions.explanation: Two carriers each pass the recessive allele with probability one half, so the chance an offspring receives two recessive alleles is one half times one half, which is 0.25.
questions.hint: Multiply the two gamete probabilities.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Describe how a recessive trait is recognised in a population
questions.stem: A written section in the report asks the team to describe how a recessive trait is recognised in a population.

answer.exemplar: A recessive trait appears only in individuals who carry two copies of the recessive allele, so unaffected carriers in the same population transmit it silently. Field workers identify such individuals by crossing them with a homozygous recessive tester: if about half the offspring show the recessive form, the untested parent is heterozygous.

questions.explanation: Recessive phenotypes appear only in homozygous individuals, so carriers must be detected indirectly. A testcross does this, because a 1:1 split of offspring reveals that the untested parent carries the allele.
questions.hint: Unaffected parents can still carry the allele.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish random deviation from a real genetic effect
questions.stem: The sampling protocol asks the team to distinguish a random deviation from a real genetic effect.

options.text: A deviation is random when the observed counts fall within what the predicted ratio allows by chance alone.
A deviation is random when the smallest class is empty, since chance often removes rare types.
options.misconception: treats a missing class as evidence of chance

options.text: A deviation is random when the totals for the two parents differ greatly from each other.
options.misconception: bases randomness on unequal parental totals

options.text: A deviation is random when the counts were gathered over a single day of trapping.
options.misconception: bases randomness on when the sample was collected

questions.explanation: A predicted ratio defines the range of counts chance alone can produce for a sample of that size. Deviations inside that range need no extra genetic explanation, while those outside it point to a real effect.
questions.hint: Ask how far chance alone could push the counts.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain equal gamete allele types in a heterozygote
questions.stem: Field staff ask why segregation guarantees that two heterozygous parents make two kinds of gamete in equal numbers.

options.text: Because each allele is copied twice during the division that produces gametes.
options.misconception: invents extra copying of alleles during gamete formation

options.text: Because the two alleles separate at meiosis and each homologue enters half of the gametes.
Because the dominant allele is needed in every cell and is therefore passed on more often.
options.misconception: ties gamete frequency to the dominant phenotype

options.text: Because the recessive allele is only copied when the cell needs a gamete.
options.misconception: claims allele copying depends on cell need

questions.explanation: Meiosis separates the paired homologous chromosomes so each gamete receives one homologue, and those homologues carry the two alleles of a heterozygote. That separation makes the two gamete types equally frequent.
questions.hint: Each homologue enters half the gametes.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Read a sample against a Punnett square prediction
questions.stem: A quadrat survey found 36 plants with purple flowers, 72 with pale flowers and 36 with white flowers in one population.

options.text: The counts match a 1:2:1 ratio, so the pale plants are heterozygotes and the two other classes are homozygotes.
The counts match a 3:1 ratio, so the pale class must be the dominant homozygotes.
options.misconception: calls the largest class the dominant homozygotes

options.text: The counts match a 9:3:3:1 ratio, so two independent genes shape the flower colour.
options.misconception: claims a dihybrid ratio from one scored trait

options.text: The counts match a 1:1 ratio, so the pale class is a separate species of plant.
options.misconception: treats an intermediate class as a separate species

questions.explanation: The 36:72:36 split matches the 1:2:1 genotypic ratio, and with two partially dominant alleles the middle class of 72 must be the heterozygotes. That is what a Punnett square predicts for two heterozygotes.
questions.hint: Match the counts to one, two and one parts.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Reject a ratio claimed from a tiny sample
questions.stem: A note is rejected because it reports a 3:1 ratio from a sample of nine offspring and treats it as proof.

options.text: The note is fine, because a ratio from nine offspring is the same evidence as a ratio from nine hundred.
options.misconception: treats sample size as irrelevant to a ratio

options.text: The note should say nine offspring are enough when the expected classes are large numbers.
options.misconception: believes a large expected class justifies a tiny sample

options.text: The note should say the ratio should be reported as percentages rather than as counts.
options.misconception: claims percentages rescue an undersized sample

options.text: The note is wrong, because nine offspring can give many different splits by chance alone.

questions.explanation: Nine offspring split into four classes can fall into many patterns by chance, so a single 3:1-looking sample proves nothing. A useful ratio test needs a sample large enough that the expected counts exceed a few individuals each.
questions.hint: Think about how many outcomes nine trials allow.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why three to one keeps appearing in plots
questions.stem: The report needs an explanation of why a three to one pattern keeps appearing in the survey plots.

answer.exemplar: The plot shows about three plants with the dominant flower colour for every one with the recessive colour, because the dominant allele is expressed in heterozygotes as well as in homozygotes. When two heterozygous plants are crossed, three quarters of the seedlings carry at least one dominant allele and so show the dominant colour.

questions.explanation: Dominance merges the homozygous dominant and heterozygous classes, together three quarters of the offspring of two heterozygotes. The recessive quarter is the homozygous class, giving the three to one split.
questions.hint: Dominance hides the difference between two genotype classes.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: State what a testcross reveals
questions.stem: A protocol asks the team to state what a testcross reveals about an untested individual.

options.text: It reveals which alleles the untested individual puts into its gametes, and so its genotype.
It reveals how many offspring the untested individual will produce in the next generation.
options.misconception: treats the testcross as a measure of fertility

options.text: It reveals whether the recessive trait is present anywhere in the wider population.
options.misconception: claims a testcross maps the whole population

options.text: It reveals the allele frequencies of the whole population from a single pair of parents.
options.misconception: believes one testcross gives population allele frequencies

questions.explanation: A testcross reads the gametes of the untested parent directly, because the recessive tester cannot hide them. It says nothing about fertility, the wider population or population allele frequencies.
questions.hint: Think about what the offspring reveal about gametes.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the product rule gives a combined class
questions.stem: Field reviewers ask why the product rule gives the frequency of a combined phenotype class.

options.text: Because the two traits are scored on the same plant, so their frequencies must be combined by adding.
options.misconception: assumes sharing a plant makes the traits dependent

options.text: Because the genes assort independently, so the chance of both traits is the product of their separate chances.
Because one trait is always rarer, and the combined class simply takes the rarer frequency.
options.misconception: believes the combined class follows the rarest trait

options.text: Because the sample size is fixed, so the combined class must be the difference of the two counts.
options.misconception: thinks combined classes come from subtracting counts

questions.explanation: Independent assortment lets the two genes combine freely, so a joint class has the product of the single-gene frequencies, giving nine sixteenths for a double dominant class. Adding or subtracting counts has no basis.
questions.hint: Independence is what licenses multiplying.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret moth counts that suggest a 3:1 split

options.misconception: names the smaller class as the recessive homozygote

options.text: The counts fit a 1:1 ratio, so the pale form must be the recessive one.
options.misconception: calls the common class recessive in a one to one split

options.text: The counts fit a 1:2:1 ratio, so the survey has scored three separate allele pairs.
options.misconception: claims a three class ratio from two visible forms

options.text: The counts fit a 3:1 ratio, so the dominant-looking moths should be three quarters of the sample.

questions.hint: Compare the counts with three quarters and one quarter.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Count heterozygous seedlings from a Punnett square
questions.stem: Another tally asks how many of 80 seedlings from two heterozygous plants should carry both allele forms.
questions.explanation: A cross of two heterozygotes gives a 1:2:1 genotypic ratio, and the heterozygous class holds two of the four parts. Two parts of 80 is 40 seedlings carrying one allele of each form.
questions.hint: Two parts of the four-part ratio.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why ratios from small samples are unreliable
questions.stem: A written answer in the report explains why ratios observed in small samples are unreliable.

answer.exemplar: Ratios describe expected proportions across many independent events, so a sample of a few dozen individuals can land well above or below the prediction by chance alone. Reliable ratio testing therefore needs a sample in which each expected class holds a reasonable number of individuals, and it must report the deviation rather than hide it.

questions.explanation: Small samples produce many possible splits, so a ratio that looks convincing may simply be luck. A sound report states the observed counts, the expected counts and the size of the deviation between them.
questions.hint: Think about how many splits a small sample allows.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why dominant traits appear in a first generation
questions.stem: A protocol asks the team to explain why a dominant phenotype is often seen in the first generation of a cross.

options.text: Because the dominant allele grows faster and is copied more often in early cells.
options.misconception: credits the dominant allele with faster copying

options.text: Because the recessive allele cannot survive the trip through a pollen grain.
options.misconception: invents pollen damage to the recessive allele

options.text: Because an offspring receiving one dominant allele shows that phenotype, even from a recessive parent.
Because recessive alleles are only expressed in plants that are several years old.
options.misconception: ties recessive expression to plant age

questions.explanation: Dominance means one copy of the allele is enough to produce the phenotype, so an offspring of a heterozygous and a recessive parent shows the dominant form. Copy speed and survival play no part.
questions.hint: One copy of the allele is enough.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why two unaffected parents produce recessive young
questions.stem: Field staff ask why two unaffected parents can produce a quarter of their young with the recessive trait.

options.text: Because the recessive allele becomes dominant in the offspring that inherit it from both parents.
options.misconception: believes recessiveness switches to dominance in offspring

options.text: Because each parent is a heterozygote in which the recessive allele is masked, and two masked alleles can pair up.
Because the recessive allele skips generations and then returns in equal numbers.
options.misconception: describes the allele as skipping generations

options.text: Because the environment switches the trait on in the offspring that inherit it.
options.misconception: blames the environment for turning the trait on

questions.explanation: Both parents can be unaffected heterozygotes in whom the recessive allele is masked. When both pass it on, the offspring receive two recessive alleles and show the trait, giving the three to one pattern.
questions.hint: Think about masked alleles meeting in one offspring.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Judge a seedling count against the 3:1 expectation
questions.stem: The survey tallied 150 seedlings and found 96 with the dominant leaf shape and 54 with the recessive shape.

options.text: The split is below the 3:1 expectation, so the sample departs from the expected proportion.
The split matches 3:1 exactly, so the field team can report a perfect Mendelian ratio.
options.misconception: treats a near match as an exact ratio

options.text: The split is above 3:1, so the recessive allele must be favoured by selection in the plot.
options.misconception: invokes selection to explain a low recessive count

options.text: The split is close to 1:1, so the cross must have been a testcross rather than a monohybrid.
options.misconception: reads a near three to one split as one to one

questions.explanation: The expected split is near 113 and 37, but the observed 96 and 54 has more recessive plants than expected. With a sample this size the difference is worth checking against sampling error.
questions.hint: Work out the expected counts before judging the split.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Correct a claim that testcross ratios never differ
questions.stem: A field note wrongly states that a testcross of an unknown plant gives the same ratio whether the unknown is homozygous or heterozygous.

options.text: The note is right, because the tester's alleles decide the outcome in every case.
options.misconception: credits the tester with deciding every outcome

options.text: The note should say the ratios differ only when the unknown plant shows the recessive form.
options.misconception: ties the outcome to the unknown plant's own colour

options.text: The note should say homozygous and heterozygous plants produce identical offspring ratios.
options.misconception: claims homozygous and heterozygous give equal results

options.text: The note is wrong, because an all dominant brood and a one to one brood mean different genotypes.

questions.explanation: A homozygous dominant unknown gives only dominant offspring, while a heterozygous unknown gives a one to one split with a recessive tester. The tester is fixed in both, so the difference comes from the unknown.
questions.hint: Work out each possible genotype separately.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Count plants carrying an allele at a given frequency
questions.stem: The report asks how many of 480 plants in a population of two alleles would be expected to carry allele a if its frequency is 0.25.
questions.explanation: The number of plants carrying the allele follows its frequency directly, so 0.25 of 480 is 120. Carriers include both heterozygotes and homozygous recessive plants, so the count is not one genotype class.
questions.hint: Multiply the allele frequency by the population size.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the chance of a recessive child from carriers
questions.stem: One question in the survey asks for the probability that two unaffected carrier parents produce a child showing the recessive trait.
questions.explanation: Each carrier passes the recessive allele with probability one half, and the two gametes combine independently, so one half times one half gives 0.25 for an offspring that shows the recessive trait.
questions.hint: Multiply the two half chances together.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Describe how a failed ratio should be reported
questions.stem: A short answer in the report explains how a field team should report a ratio that fails to match.

answer.exemplar: A failing ratio is reported honestly, with the observed class counts, the expected counts from the ratio, and the size and direction of the difference. The team should then consider sampling error first, and only then look for biological causes such as incomplete dominance, linkage, selection or misidentified plants in the field.

questions.explanation: Reporting a mismatch means giving the observed counts, the expected counts and the deviation, then checking sampling error before biology. Hiding a failed ratio weakens the survey.
questions.hint: Report counts, expectation and deviation together.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: State the condition for independent assortment
questions.stem: A requirement in the protocol states the condition under which two traits can be predicted independently.

options.text: The two genes must be on different chromosomes, or far apart on the same one.
The two traits must be scored on separate plants during separate visits.
options.misconception: links independence to how the survey is scheduled

options.text: The two genes must have exactly the same allele frequency in the population.
options.misconception: claims independence needs matching allele frequencies

options.text: The two traits must be visible at the same stage of the plants' growth.
options.misconception: ties genetic independence to a growth stage

questions.explanation: Independent assortment happens when the genes are on separate chromosomes or far apart on the same chromosome, so their gametes combine at random. Survey timing, allele frequencies and growth stage have no effect on inheritance.
questions.hint: It depends on the position of the two genes.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a Punnett square gives proportions
questions.stem: Field reviewers ask why a Punnett square predicts proportions rather than actual offspring.

options.text: Because a Punnett square records the offspring already counted in the field.
options.misconception: treats the square as a record of counted offspring

options.text: Because it lists the possible gamete pairings, and the proportions follow from how likely each pairing is.
Because each cell in the square stands for one real plant in the plot.
options.misconception: claims each cell represents an actual plant

options.text: Because the square is drawn after the seedlings have been scored.
options.misconception: claims the square is drawn from finished results

questions.explanation: A Punnett square is a table of possibilities, not a record of organisms, so it gives expected proportions based on the gamete combinations. Real broods vary around those expectations because pairing is random.
questions.hint: It is a table of possibilities, not a count.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Compare ratios from two separate samples
questions.stem: Two ponds were sampled and the results were 41 pale and 19 dark in the first, and 60 pale and 20 dark in the second.

options.text: Both samples fit a 3:1 ratio, so the field team can report a confirmed three to one pattern.
options.misconception: accepts both samples as confirming a three to one ratio

options.text: The first sample fits a 1:1 ratio while the second fits a 3:1 ratio, so the ponds differ genetically.
options.misconception: reads one split as one to one and the other as three to one

options.text: The second sample fits a 1:2:1 ratio, so three allele classes must be present in that pond.
options.misconception: claims a three class ratio from two visible forms

options.text: Both samples are near 2:1, so neither matches a 3:1 expectation and both need checking.

questions.explanation: Both ponds give about two pale moths for every dark one, while a 3:1 expectation would need roughly 45 pale and 15 dark in a sample of 60. Neither sample matches the expected ratio, so both need further checking.
questions.hint: Compute the ratio in each sample separately.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Correct a claim that dominant forms are always commoner
questions.stem: A claim in the survey asserts that the dominant form must always be the more common one in a population.

options.text: The claim holds, because dominant alleles are always more frequent than recessive alleles.
options.misconception: believes dominance guarantees greater allele frequency

options.text: The claim should say the common form is dominant whenever the population is not inbred.
options.misconception: ties commonness to dominance in a general population

options.text: The claim is wrong, because a recessive allele can be common when the dominant one is rare or harmful.
The claim should say the two forms are always equally common in any large population.
options.misconception: claims the two forms must always be equally common

questions.explanation: Dominance describes expression in a heterozygote, not how common an allele is in a population. A recessive allele can be frequent, while a dominant one can be rare if it is disadvantageous or newly arisen.
questions.hint: Frequency and expression are different things.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the expected number of carriers
questions.stem: A calculation in the report asks for the expected number of carriers among 300 offspring of two heterozygous parents.
questions.explanation: Half of the offspring of two heterozygotes are heterozygous, because the 1:2:1 genotypic ratio puts two parts in that class. Half of 300 is 150 plants that carry the recessive allele without showing it.
questions.hint: Carriers make up half of that cross.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Count the recessive quarter of a sample
questions.stem: A count in the notebook asks how many of 240 seedlings from two heterozygous parents should show the recessive trait.
questions.explanation: The recessive class is one quarter of the offspring of two heterozygotes, since only the homozygous recessive group shows the trait. One quarter of 240 is 60 seedlings.
questions.hint: One quarter of the offspring show the recessive trait.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Describe how testcross results are interpreted
questions.stem: One model answer in the report states how the results of a testcross are interpreted.

answer.exemplar: Cross the unknown individual with a homozygous recessive tester and score the offspring for the dominant and recessive forms. If every offspring shows the dominant form, the unknown was homozygous dominant. If the offspring split roughly one to one, the unknown was heterozygous and passed on the recessive allele to half of its gametes.

questions.explanation: The tester contributes only recessive alleles, so dominant offspring prove the unknown supplied a dominant allele. An all dominant brood means homozygous dominant; a one to one split means heterozygous.
questions.hint: Read the offspring against the tester phenotype.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: State how alleles relate to one gene
questions.stem: Field reviewers want a statement about how alleles relate to a single gene in a population.

options.text: Each allele is a separate gene that controls a different trait in the population.
options.misconception: treats each allele as a separate gene

options.text: Each allele is an extra copy of the gene produced only in homozygous individuals.
options.misconception: claims alleles are extra copies made in homozygotes

options.text: Each allele is one of the versions of the same gene that the population carries.
Each allele is the visible trait that the gene produces in the environment.
options.misconception: describes alleles as visible traits

questions.explanation: An allele is a version of one gene, and a population can carry several versions at the same locus while any individual carries only two. Alleles are not separate genes, extra copies or visible traits.
questions.hint: One gene, several versions of it.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how recessive alleles persist in a population
questions.stem: Field staff ask how a recessive allele can persist in a population for many generations.

options.text: Because recessive alleles are copied more often than dominant ones during gamete formation.
options.misconception: credits recessive alleles with extra copying

options.text: Because heterozygotes hide it from selection, so it can be carried along unseen.
Because recessive alleles change into dominant alleles when the population is disturbed.
options.misconception: claims alleles switch dominance when disturbed

options.text: Because every generation must contain at least one individual showing the recessive form.
options.misconception: claims the form must always be visible somewhere

questions.explanation: Recessive alleles can hide inside heterozygotes, where selection cannot reach them, so they persist even when the dominant form is common. They can also vanish if no carrier remains.
questions.hint: Think about alleles hidden in heterozygotes.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Compare counts with the three to one expectation
questions.stem: The tally lists 200 individuals of which 150 show the dominant form and 50 show the recessive form.

options.text: The counts match the 3:1 expectation, so the sample is consistent with two heterozygous parents.
The counts match a 1:1 ratio, so the survey should record the population as homozygous.
options.misconception: calls a three to one split a one to one split

options.text: The counts match a 1:2:1 ratio, so three separate genotype classes were scored.
options.misconception: claims a genotypic ratio from two phenotype classes

options.text: The counts match a 9:3:3:1 ratio, so two genes must be segregating in the population.
options.misconception: claims a dihybrid ratio from one scored trait

questions.explanation: Three quarters of 200 is 150 and one quarter is 50, exactly the counts recorded, so the sample agrees with the 3:1 expectation for two heterozygous parents. Agreement supports that cross without proving it.
questions.hint: Compare the counts with three quarters of the total.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Correct the ratio produced by a testcross
questions.stem: A note states that a heterozygous plant crossed with a recessive one gives a 3:1 ratio of the two forms.

options.text: The note is right, because half the gametes carry each allele and one quarter pair up.
options.misconception: applies a monohybrid ratio to a testcross

options.text: The note should say the ratio appears only if the recessive parent is heterozygous too.
options.misconception: requires the tester to be heterozygous as well

options.text: The note should say the ratio appears only when the two plants are of different species.
options.misconception: invents a species requirement for the ratio

options.text: The note is wrong, because this cross gives a 1:1 ratio rather than a 3:1 ratio.

questions.explanation: A heterozygote crossed with a homozygous recessive gives half dominant and half recessive offspring, since every gamete from the recessive parent carries the recessive allele. That is the one to one testcross ratio.
questions.hint: Work out the gamete types from each parent.

questions.learningObjective: Count gametes carrying the recessive allele
questions.stem: One estimate in the report asks how many of 500 gametes from a heterozygous plant carry the recessive allele.
questions.explanation: Segregation sends one homologue into each gamete, so half the gametes of a heterozygote carry the recessive allele. Half of 500 is 250 gametes, which is the figure the survey expects.
questions.hint: Half of the gametes carry it.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the recessive class in a small sample
questions.stem: The calculation in the notebook asks how many of 120 offspring should show the recessive trait in a cross of two heterozygotes.
questions.explanation: The recessive class is one quarter of the offspring of two heterozygotes, since only the homozygous recessive group shows the trait. One quarter of 120 is 30 seedlings.
questions.hint: One quarter of the offspring show the recessive trait.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish dominance from commonness
questions.stem: A short written answer explains why dominance must not be confused with commonness in a population.

answer.exemplar: Dominance describes how an allele is expressed when it is paired with another allele in a heterozygote, whereas commonness describes how often that allele occurs in the population. A rare dominant allele can dominate a heterozygote, and a common recessive allele can stay hidden inside carriers, so the two ideas must be kept apart in any survey report.

questions.explanation: Dominance concerns expression within an individual, while commonness concerns allele frequency in a population. The two can point in opposite directions, so a report must never infer one from the other.
questions.hint: One describes expression, the other frequency.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Define a carrier of a recessive allele
questions.stem: The field supervisor wants a correct statement about carriers of a recessive allele.

options.text: A carrier carries one recessive allele but shows the dominant phenotype, because the allele is masked.
A carrier shows the recessive phenotype, because the recessive allele is expressed on its own.
options.misconception: confuses a carrier with an affected individual

options.text: A carrier carries two recessive alleles and shows the recessive phenotype in most plants.
options.misconception: describes a carrier as homozygous recessive

options.text: A carrier carries the dominant allele twice and shows a weakened recessive phenotype.
options.misconception: invents a weakened phenotype for a dominant homozygote

questions.explanation: A carrier is heterozygous, holding one recessive allele that is masked by the dominant allele beside it, so the dominant phenotype shows. Showing the recessive phenotype requires two copies of the recessive allele.
questions.hint: Ask how many copies of the recessive allele are present.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how segregation produces the 3:1 pattern
questions.stem: Field reviewers ask how the 3:1 pattern of a field cross arises from the segregation of one gene.

options.text: Each parent contributes a dominant allele to three offspring in four, because it is copied more often.
options.misconception: credits the dominant allele with more copying

options.text: Each parent makes half dominant and half recessive gametes, so a quarter of the offspring get two recessives.
The recessive offspring arise only when the environment cools below the threshold for the trait.
options.misconception: blames a temperature threshold for the recessive class

options.text: The pattern arises because recessive alleles move between offspring after fertilisation takes place.
options.misconception: invokes allele movement after fertilisation

questions.explanation: Segregation means each parent produces equal numbers of gametes carrying either allele. Random pairing gives one quarter of offspring two recessive alleles, the recessive quarter of the three to one pattern.
questions.hint: Half the gametes of each parent carry it.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Deduce the genotypes of testcross offspring
questions.stem: A trapping log records genotypes for 80 offspring of a cross between a heterozygous plant and a recessive tester.

options.text: All 80 offspring must be heterozygous, since each receives one allele from each parent.
Half the offspring must show the recessive form, so the cross is a testcross of two heterozygotes.
options.misconception: claims a testcross can have two heterozygous parents

options.text: One quarter of the offspring must be homozygous recessive, matching a 3:1 pattern.
options.misconception: applies a three to one pattern to a testcross

options.text: The offspring must show a 1:1 ratio, since the unknown parent makes two gamete types.
options.misconception: misses that the tester fixes the recessive allele always

questions.explanation: The recessive tester contributes a recessive allele to every offspring, and the heterozygous parent contributes each allele equally, so every offspring is heterozygous and shows the dominant form.
questions.hint: Add the allele from each parent.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Correct a claim about how many alleles an individual holds
questions.stem: One claim in the survey asserts that each individual in a population can carry only two alleles of a gene.

options.text: The claim holds, because every individual has exactly two chromosome sets.
options.misconception: extends a diploid limit to whole populations

options.text: The claim should say individuals can carry only one allele in wild populations.
options.misconception: claims individuals hold a single allele in the wild

options.text: The claim should say the number of alleles per individual depends on the number of gene pairs.
options.misconception: ties allele count to the number of gene pairs

options.text: The claim is wrong, because an individual carries two alleles while a population can carry many more.

questions.explanation: Each diploid individual holds two copies of a gene, but a population can carry many alleles at the same locus and any two can pair up in an individual. The limit of two applies per individual, not per population.
questions.hint: Separate the individual from the population.
